etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English tiklen, tikelen, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a frequentative form of Middle English tikken (“to touch lightly”), thus equivalent to tick +‎ -le; or perhaps related to Old English tinclian (“to tickle”). Compare North Frisian tigele (“to tickle”) (Hallig dialect), and tiikle (“to tickle”) (Amrum dialect), German dialectal zicklen (“to excite; stir up”).
Alternatively, from a metathetic alteration of Middle English kitelen ("to tickle"; see kittle).

definitions.definition: An itchy feeling resembling the result of tickling.
(cricket, informal) A light tap of the ball.

quote.text: There's a very fine line between a tickle and an edge!

definitions.definition: (Newfoundland) A narrow strait, such as between an island and the shore.

quote.citation: 1903 April 8, The Syren and Shipping, page 169:
quote.text: Charts and Plans. [...] No. New Charts. 2253 England, and south coast—Dartmouth harbour. [...] 3320 Newfoundland, Thimble tickles and Glover harbour—Head of Seal bay.

quote.citation: 2004, Richard Fortey, The Earth, Folio Society, published 2011, page 169:
quote.text: Cow Head itself is a prominent headland connected to the settlement by a natural causeway, or ‘tickle’ as the Newfoundlanders prefer it.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To touch repeatedly or stroke delicately in a manner which causes laughter, pleasure and twitching.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: If you tickle us, do we not laugh?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To unexpectedly touch or stroke delicately in a manner which causes displeasure or withdrawal.
(intransitive, of a body part) To feel as if the body part in question is being tickled.
(transitive) To appeal to someone's taste, curiosity etc.
(transitive) To cause delight or amusement in.

quote.citation: 1733, Alexander Pope, “Epistle II”, in An Essay on Man, lines 275–276; republished in The Complete Poetical Works of Alexander Pope, Boston, New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1902, page 145:
quote.text: Behold the child, by Nature's kindly law,Pleas'd with a rattle, tickled with a straw.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: Such a natureTickled with good success, disdains the shadowWhich he treads on at noon.

quote.citation: 1591, Ed[mund] Sp[enser], “Muiopotmos, or The Fate of the Butterflie”, in Complaints. Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie. […], London:  […]  William Ponsonbie, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: He with secret joy thereforeDid tickle inwardly in every vein.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To catch fish in the hand (usually in rivers or smaller streams) by manually stimulating the fins.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto IV”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: So ticle be the termes of mortall state,And full of subtile sophismes, which do playWith double senses, and with false debate  […]

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Measure for Measure”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: Lucio. I warrant it is: And thy head stands so tickle onthy shoulders, that a milke-maid, if she be in loue, maysigh it off: Send after the Duke, and appeale to him.
